There are various single-stage presses which are sold as kits for people who are just starting out. Lee, Dillion, Rockchucker, and others make nice entry-level setups. My advice is to pick the one you like best and just dive in.

Once you get into it, you'll learn what you need and what you like, and you'll slowly replace all your starter equipment with new stuff. That's the best way. You can't just dive in with high-end gear and hope that you guessed right about everything before you even begin.

I have four pieces of specific advice:

  • Be methodical and careful. Almost every blown-up gun on the internet got blown up by a reloading mistake. Take it seriously and take your time.

  • Every reloader - every single one - gets their gear set up and then realizes that their workspace is too small. Set your spot up with plenty of room, plenty of shelves and drawers, and a nice firm stable bench to put the press on. It does not have to be fancy, it just has to be strong enough not to flex.

  • The golden rule: One can of powder at a time. Keep your gunpowder in another room. Go get one can, use it, and put it back in the other room before getting a second one. If everybody followed this rule the accident rate would probably be cut in half.

  • The other golden rule: Never use a recipe that fills a case less than half way with powder. Why? So an accidental double-charge will overflow, rather than risk going undetected. If everybody followed this rule too, the accident rate would probably be a tenth of what it is now.

Don't let the accident talk scare you off, if you can handle a gun safely you're conscientious enough to be a good safe reloader too. It's fun and it opens up a whole new world. One day you'll be at a gun show and you'll find lovely old rifle that's dirt cheap because it uses some weirdball cartridge. You'll buy the rifle, some dies, work up a nice mild load that's comfortable and fun to shoot, and you'll have a blast shooting cheap ammo out of an excellent gun forever. It's very rewarding stuff.

Reloading, much like golf, fishing, racecars and hookers can be a very expensive habit and hobby. Before you jump in with both feet consider what your goal(s) are. If you don't have a specific need in mind, and one that can help you recover investments, it may not be for you. Even if you go with a lower cost single-stage [press/kit], by the time you get a press, die, caliper, trimmer, tumbler, books, primers, powder, etc. etc. etc. you can have a very significant investment. Even in the single-stage world you can invest over $1k just to get started. Just bump that on up a couple times if you want to go progressive and use an electronic powder measure ... and you will.

If you only shoot every now and then (8 or 9 times a year) you are probably better off just buying ammo. Hit the sales and gun shows and stock up. You have to shoot a considerable amount just to recoup your investment.

If you are doing some long-term planning, or want to get in to competition and roll your own precision loads, then just start collecting the pieces and parts over time. Before you know it you'll have a tool set and be ready to rock.

I shoot a lot but still prefer my single stage RCBS Rock Chucker. It is a solid and reliable machine. I reload out of necessity but also as a hobby - I'm never in a hurry and crank out a couple hundred rounds whenever the mood strikes me. I always have plenty on hand. Sitting down and working the press is a great stress reliever and I love doing it. The single-stage also keeps me engaged - I have to think about and watch every step. This is not something you want to do half-assed; you can, and will, get hurt or hurt someone else. It's a specific and detailed process and you need to pay attention.

A progressive press is awesome and you can crank out some rounds, but it is much more expensive to get in to.

Think about it, research some more, and good luck!

Goal? Easy - reload what I can so I can go to the range more frequently than I do and not burn holes in my pocket. Very helpful for just about any caliber. I use a lot of 9mm, 5.56/.223, and I would do more .38 but the local gun stores are scalpers. After a bit I might get into reloading shot shells - not for the cost but for the fun (confetti shot anyone?)

Go for it! I still like a single-stage press but that is a personal preference - mainly because I just like to sit in my little shop and take my time. I also have two singles setup side-by side. I use one just for depriming/resizing. The other I use for all the other functions. I will say this though, I went to a friends house to help load some 5.56 in a hurry for some #bangbang the next day - he had the brass prepped and we knocked out a couple thousand rounds in a just a few hours with his Dillon XL 650. That thing is a beast - once it was setup we rolled in a hurry.

For shotshell - that's the one you can get in to quick and cheap. I have a Lee Load All for 12ga and it was the best $49 I've spent. I have a line on a MEC 600 Jr. and I'm going to get it soon. I love loading shotshell and it's far and away the cheapest "get-in" for loading.

Good luck and do take your time when you get started - make sure your recipes are right and you do all the steps in the right order. Check, recheck and check again. Once you get rolling you will enjoy it.
